questions.question: Which literary editor of 'The Spectator' anonymously published the 1 October 1954 leader article 'In the Movement', giving the 1950s poetic group its name?
questions.explanation: Spectator literary editor J D Scott wrote the unsigned October 1954 article In the Movement declaring that a tough-minded anti-romantic generation had arrived.

questions.question: Which poet was the sole female contributor included among the nine poets in Robert Conquest's landmark 1956 Movement anthology 'New Lines'?
questions.explanation: Elizabeth Jennings was the only woman among the nine poets in New Lines 1956 alongside Larkin Amis Wain Davie Enright Holloway Gunn and Conquest.

questions.question: Which 1957 anthology, edited by Dannie Abse and Howard Sergeant to oppose the dry academic restraint of 'New Lines', championed Dionysian emotional energy?
questions.explanation: Abse and Sergeant edited Mavericks in 1957 featuring David Wright Jon Silkin and J C Hall as a neo-romantic counter-manifesto to The Movement.

questions.question: Which London poetry workshop—founded by Philip Hobsbaum in 1955 and hosted later by Edward Lucie-Smith—nurtured poets such as Peter Porter and George MacBeth?
questions.explanation: Meeting every Friday evening to subject cyclostyled poems to rigorous oral critique The Group published A Group Anthology in 1963.

questions.question: Which three pop-influenced performance poets from Liverpool were featured in the bestselling 1967 Penguin Modern Poets 10 volume 'The Mersey Sound'?
options: Adrian Henri, Roger McGough, and Brian Patten
Christopher Logue, Michael Horovitz, and Pete Brown
Tony Harrison, Douglas Dunn, and Sean O'Brien
Linton Kwesi Johnson, Benjamin Zephaniah, and John Agard
questions.explanation: Published in 1967 Penguin Modern Poets 10 The Mersey Sound brought together the Liverpool Poets Adrian Henri Roger McGough and Brian Patten.

questions.question: Under what female pseudonym did the young Philip Larkin write two boarding-school novellas ('Trouble at Willow Gables' and 'Michaelmas Term at St Brides') in 1943?
questions.explanation: In 1943 Larkin invented the persona of the spinster writer Brunette Coleman authoring two girls school stories a pseudo-autobiography and French symbolist poems.

questions.question: From which Shakespearean play and scene does Philip Larkin's 1955 poetry collection 'The Less Deceived' take its title?
options: Measure for Measure, Act IV, Scene 1
questions.explanation: When Hamlet tells Ophelia I loved you not she replies I was the more deceived prompting Larkin title The Less Deceived.

questions.question: From which fourteenth-century Middle English alliterative romance did Ted Hughes take both the title and the epigraph of his 1967 collection 'Wodwo'?
options: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
questions.explanation: In Fitt II of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight Gawain battles wodwos or wild forest men that dwelt in the cliffs.

questions.question: Which 1971 sequence of thirty prose-hymns by Geoffrey Hill superimposes the eighth-century Anglo-Saxon king of Mercia onto the poet's Worcestershire childhood?
questions.explanation: Geoffrey Hill Mercian Hymns 1971 blends King Offa eighth-century earthworks and coinage with memories of mid-twentieth-century Bromsgrove nail-making.

questions.question: Which 1985 poem in abab quatrains by Tony Harrison—written during the Miners' Strike after skinheads spray-painted his parents' gravestone in Leeds—caused a major uproar on Channel 4?
questions.explanation: Modeled on Gray Elegy Tony Harrison poem V explores class division versus and victory after finding UNITED sprayed on the family grave at Beeston Hill.

questions.question: In Seamus Heaney's bog poem 'The Tollund Man' (1972), to which Danish city does the speaker vow he will travel ('Some day I will go to ______ / To see his peat-brown head')?
questions.explanation: Confusing Silkeborg Museum with nearby Aarhus Museum Heaney opened The Tollund Man with Some day I will go to Aarhus To see his peat-brown head.

questions.question: What is the title of the eight-sonnet sequence in 'The Haw Lantern' (1987) that Seamus Heaney composed in memory of his mother, Margaret Kathleen Heaney?
questions.explanation: Prefaced by a poem on a chestnut tree Clearances contains the famous Sonnet 3 When all the others were away at Mass I was all hers as we peeled potatoes.

questions.question: In Derek Walcott's 1990 Caribbean epic 'Omeros', written in loose three-line stanzas, which two St. Lucian fishermen compete for the housemaid Helen?
questions.explanation: In Omeros the St Lucian canoe-fisherman Achille and the passenger-van driver Hector vie for the proud pregnant housemaid Helen.

questions.question: Which three novels, originally written by Samuel Beckett in French between 1947 and 1950 before he translated them into English, form his postwar 'Trilogy'?
options: Murphy, Watt, and Mercier and Camier
More Pricks Than Kicks, Murphy, and How It Is
Company, Ill Seen Ill Said, and Worstward Ho
Molloy, Malone Dies, and The Unnamable
questions.explanation: Published in French in 1951-1953 and collected in English in 1959 Molloy Malone Dies and The Unnamable progressively strip away plot body and ego.

questions.question: In Act I of Samuel Beckett's 'Waiting for Godot', what physical action prompts the mute servant Lucky to launch into his torrential, unpunctuated philosophical speech?
options: Handing him a raw turnip and a half-gnawed chicken bone
Untying the heavy rope from around his bleeding neck
Striking his boots three times with Pozzo's whip
Placing Lucky's bowler hat upon his head and commanding him to 'Think!'
questions.explanation: Pozzo explains that Lucky cannot think without his hat; when Vladimir places the bowler hat on Lucky head he erupts into his speech on a personal God with a white beard.

questions.question: In Samuel Beckett's 1958 one-man play 'Krapp's Last Tape', how old is the solitary protagonist Krapp as he listens on his birthday to a spool recorded by his thirty-nine-year-old self?
questions.explanation: On his sixty-ninth birthday Krapp listens to Box Three Spool Five recorded at age thirty-nine which itself mocks a tape made at age twenty-seven.

questions.question: In Samuel Beckett's 1961 two-act play 'Happy Days', what is the physical predicament of the cheerful protagonist Winnie across Acts I and II?
options: She is strapped to a mechanical rocking chair that rocks faster whenever a bell rings
She is sealed inside a large grey funerary urn alongside her husband's mistress
She is buried up to her waist in a scorching mound in Act I, and up to her neck in Act II
She is suspended in a wire cage five feet above a flooded stage
questions.explanation: Awakened by a piercing bell Winnie rummages in her black bag while buried to the waist in Act I and can move only her eyes and lips when buried to the neck in Act II.

questions.question: From the subtitle of which 1957 play by David Campton did theatre critic Irving Wardle borrow the phrase 'Comedy of Menace' to describe Harold Pinter's early drama?
questions.explanation: Irving Wardle borrowed the phrase from David Campton 1957 play The Lunatic View A Comedy of Menace for his September 1958 Encore review of Pinter.

questions.question: In Harold Pinter's 1965 play 'The Homecoming', who is the philosophy professor who brings his wife Ruth to his father Max's North London house, only to return to America without her?
questions.explanation: Doctor of Philosophy Teddy passively watches as his wife Ruth agrees to stay behind in North London as housekeeper and Madonna-whore to Max Lenny and Joey.

questions.question: At which fictional Derbyshire country estate is Tom Stoppard's 1993 play 'Arcadia' set, alternating scenes between 1809–1812 and the present day?
questions.explanation: Set in a single garden room at Sidley Park in Derbyshire Arcadia juxtaposes Thomasina Coverly and Septimus Hodge in 1809 with Hannah Jarvis and Bernard Nightingale.

questions.question: How much historical time elapses between Act I (set in Victorian colonial Africa) and Act II (set in a London park in 1979) of Caryl Churchill's 'Cloud Nine', although the characters age only twenty-five years?
questions.explanation: Between Act I and Act II a century of historical time passes from Victorian Africa to 1979 London while Betty Edward and Victoria age only twenty-five years.

questions.question: In what kind of rural Irish school in the fictional Donegal parish of Baile Beag in August 1833 is Brian Friel's 'Translations' (1980) set?
questions.explanation: Master Hugh O Donnell teaches Latin Greek and Irish in a barn hedge-school at Baile Beag as British Royal Engineers arrive to map and rename the countryside.

questions.question: At which London theatre venue did twenty-three-year-old Sarah Kane's controversial debut play 'Blasted' premiere in January 1995?
questions.explanation: Staged before sixty-five seats at the Royal Court Theatre Upstairs in January 1995 Sarah Kane Blasted ignited the biggest critical storm since Bond Saved.

questions.question: What is the subject of the hilariously pedantic academic article that probationary history lecturer Jim Dixon struggles to publish in Kingsley Amis's 'Lucky Jim' (1954)?
options: The economic influence of developments in shipbuilding techniques, 1450 to 1485
The agrarian enclosure of seventeenth-century Leicestershire
The wool-trade tariffs of the Hanseatic League under Henry VII
The liturgical reforms of Archbishop Laud in provincial cathedrals
questions.explanation: Jim Dixon opens his article The Economic Influence of the Developments in Shipbuilding Techniques 1450 to 1485 with the phrase In considering this strangely neglected topic.

questions.question: Whose sudden appearance on the beach at the very end of William Golding's 'Lord of the Flies' (1954) halts Jack's hunters as they pursue Ralph through the burning island?
options: A party of Polynesian pearl fishermen
A British naval officer from a passing cruiser
A missionary priest in a motor launch
A downed Royal Air Force fighter pilot
questions.explanation: Attracted by the smoke of Jack fire a naval officer in white drill uniform and gold-buttoned cap steps ashore asking the savages if they are having a war.

questions.question: In Doris Lessing's 'The Golden Notebook' (1962), into which four colored notebooks does the writer Anna Wulf divide her experience before uniting them in the fifth golden notebook?
questions.explanation: Anna Wulf keeps a Black notebook on her African novel a Red notebook on communism a Yellow notebook for her fictional alter ego Ella and a Blue diary.

questions.question: In Chapter 61 of John Fowles's 'The French Lieutenant's Woman' (1969), outside whose real historical house at 16 Cheyne Walk in Chelsea does the intrusive author turn back his watch to switch endings?
questions.explanation: Sarah Woodruff has found shelter as assistant and model in the bohemian Chelsea household of Dante Gabriel Rossetti at 16 Tudor House Cheyne Walk.

questions.question: Who is the egotistical retired theatre director who retreats to a remote coastal house called Shruff End and kidnaps his childhood sweetheart Hartley in Iris Murdoch's 'The Sea, The Sea' (1978)?
questions.explanation: Playwright and Prospero-like director Charles Arrowby retires to write his memoirs by the sea only to unleash destructive romantic obsession.

questions.question: To which devoted pickle-factory worker—who serves as his skeptical, interrupting listener at the Braganza Pickles factory—does Saleem Sinai read aloud the thirty chapters of 'Midnight's Children' (1981)?
questions.explanation: Named after the dung-lotus goddess Padma Mangroli stirs vats of chutney by day and listens impatiently to Saleem narrative by night.

questions.question: Who is the violent military rival with crushingly powerful knees with whom Saleem Sinai was secretly swapped at birth by the nurse Mary Pereira at midnight on 15 August 1947?
questions.explanation: To please her radical lover Joseph D Costa nurse Mary Pereira switches the rich baby of Ahmed and Amina Sinai with the poor baby of Wee Willie Winkie and Vanita.

questions.question: Who is the fifty-two-year-old history teacher who abandons the French Revolution syllabus to tell his pupil Price the dark family history of the Cricks in the East Anglian Fens in Graham Swift's 'Waterland' (1983)?
questions.explanation: After his wife Mary kidnaps a baby from a supermarket history teacher Tom Crick weaves together eel-trapping silt-reclamation and family tragedy in the Fens.

questions.question: Who is the gluttonous, self-destructive thirty-five-year-old commercial director who shuttles between New York and London in Martin Amis's 1984 novel 'Money: A Suicide Note'?
questions.explanation: Addicted to fast food pornography alcohol and slot machines John Self is conned in an elaborate transatlantic film financing fraud by Fielding Goodney.

questions.question: What is the subject of the unnumbered half-chapter titled 'Parenthesis' in Julian Barnes's 'A History of the World in 10½ Chapters' (1989)?
options: A philosophical meditation on human love as the only counter-weight to history
A satirical taxonomy of woodworm species aboard Noah's Ark
A transcript of the medieval ecclesiastical trial of timber beetles
An astronaut's diary of discovering the remains of the Ark on Mount Ararat
questions.explanation: Speaking in his own voice in the unnumbered half-chapter Parenthesis Barnes argues that love is our only fragile defense against the history of the world.

questions.question: In Chapter 5 of Julian Barnes's 'A History of the World in 10½ Chapters' (1989), which famous 1819 French Romantic painting by Théodore Géricault is analyzed to show how catastrophe becomes art?
questions.explanation: Chapter 5 Shipwreck first recounts the 1816 wreck of the French frigate Medusa and then examines how Géricault sanitized starvation and cannibalism into art.

questions.question: How are the eight chapters of Jeanette Winterson's 1985 semi-autobiographical debut novel 'Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit' titled and structured?
options: After eight Arthurian knights of the Round Table
After the first eight books of the Old Testament, from Genesis to Ruth
After the eight deadly sins of early Christian desert monasticism
After the eight canonical hours of the medieval monastic liturgy
questions.explanation: Winterson titles the eight chapters Genesis Exodus Leviticus Numbers Deuteronomy Joshua Judges and Ruth interweaving fairy tales with Jeanette evangelical upbringing.

questions.question: In Kazuo Ishiguro's 'The Remains of the Day' (1989), what is the name of the grand Oxfordshire country house where the butler Stevens served the Nazi-appeasing Lord Darlington?
questions.explanation: In July 1956 Stevens borrows his new American employer Mr Farraday Ford motorcar to drive from Darlington Hall to the West Country to meet Miss Kenton.

questions.question: In the final 'London, 1999' postscript of Ian McEwan's 'Atonement' (2001), what devastating metafictional truth does the elderly novelist Briony Tallis reveal about Cecilia and Robbie Turner?
options: That the entire accusation of 1935 was a fictional plot invented for her first play
That Robbie survived the war to become a celebrated neurologist at St. Thomas's Hospital
That Cecilia married Paul Marshall after Robbie defected to the Soviet Union
That they were never reunited: Robbie died at Dunkirk and Cecilia died in the Blitz in 1940
questions.explanation: Suffering from vascular dementia Briony admits that Robbie died of septicaemia at Bray-Dunes on 1 June 1940 and Cecilia died in the Balham Tube bombing in September 1940.

questions.question: Which 1995 novel—the concluding volume of Pat Barker's World War I trilogy centering on Billy Prior and Dr. W. H. R. Rivers—won the Booker Prize?
questions.explanation: Following Regeneration 1991 and The Eye in the Door 1993 Pat Barker won the 1995 Booker Prize for The Ghost Road in which Billy Prior dies with Wilfred Owen at the Sambre-Oise Canal.

questions.question: Which three novels by Chinua Achebe trace the history of colonial Nigeria from the pre-colonial Igbo village of Umuofia through the 1920s and 1950s as 'The African Trilogy'?
options: Things Fall Apart, A Man of the People, and Anthills of the Savannah
Arrow of God, Girls at War, and There Was a Country
Things Fall Apart, The Concubine, and The Famished Road
Things Fall Apart, No Longer at Ease, and Arrow of God
questions.explanation: Things Fall Apart 1958 portrays Okonkwo No Longer at Ease 1960 portrays his grandson Obi Okonkwo in 1950s Lagos and Arrow of God 1964 portrays the chief priest Ezeulu.

questions.question: In Jean Rhys's 1966 postcolonial prequel to 'Jane Eyre', 'Wide Sargasso Sea', what is the true childhood name of the white Creole heiress from Jamaica before her husband renames her 'Bertha'?
questions.explanation: Raised at Coulibri Estate in post-emancipation Jamaica Antoinette Cosway is stripped of her dowry sanity and name by her English husband.

questions.question: In J. M. Coetzee's 1986 metafictional reworking of 'Robinson Crusoe', 'Foe', why is the African servant Friday completely unable to tell Susan Barton or Daniel Foe his own story?
options: He has taken a lifelong monastic vow of silence after the shipwreck
His tongue has been cut out
He speaks only an extinct dialect of the interior Andes
He was born deaf and mute on the coast of Brazil
questions.explanation: Cruso tells Susan Barton that slavers cut out Friday tongue leaving Friday silenced at the mute center of the colonial archive.

questions.question: Who is the fifty-two-year-old Cape Town professor of Romantic poetry who loses his university post over an affair with a student and retreats to his daughter Lucy's farm in J. M. Coetzee's 'Disgrace' (1999)?
questions.explanation: While writing an opera on Lord Byron and Teresa Guiccioli David Lurie refuses to make a contrite public confession and witnesses a brutal attack on Lucy farm in the Eastern Cape.

questions.question: Who is the entrepreneurial chauffeur from the 'Darkness' of Laxmangarh village who murders his employer Mr. Ashok and writes seven nocturnal letters to Premier Wen Jiabao in Aravind Adiga's 'The White Tiger' (2008)?
questions.explanation: Nicknamed the White Tiger by a school inspector Balram Halwai kills his master Ashok with a Johnny Walker bottle steals 700000 rupees and starts a taxi company in Bangalore.

questions.question: Which 2019 dystopian sequel to her 1985 novel 'The Handmaid's Tale'—narrated partly by Aunt Lydia—won Margaret Atwood her second Booker Prize?
questions.explanation: Set fifteen years after The Handmaid Tale Margaret Atwood The Testaments jointly won the 2019 Booker Prize alongside Bernardine Evaristo Girl Woman Other.

questions.question: In which year was the Nagasaki-born British novelist Kazuo Ishiguro awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature?
questions.explanation: Kazuo Ishiguro received the 2017 Nobel Prize in Literature for novels of great emotional force such as The Remains of the Day and Never Let Me Go.

questions.question: Which Zanzibar-born British novelist—author of 'Paradise' (1994), 'By the Sea' (2001), and 'Afterlives' (2020)—was awarded the 2021 Nobel Prize in Literature?
questions.explanation: Emeritus Professor at the University of Kent Abdulrazak Gurnah won the 2021 Nobel Prize for his compassionate exploration of colonialism and the refugee experience.

questions.question: Which 1990 comic coming-of-age novel by Hanif Kureishi opens with the famous line 'My name is Karim Amir, and I am an Englishman born and bred, almost'?
questions.explanation: Winner of the Whitbread First Novel Award in 1990 The Buddha of Suburbia follows the mixed-race teenager Karim Amir from Bromley to 1970s London theatre.

questions.question: Which 2003 debut novel by Monica Ali chronicles the life of Nazneen, a young Bangladeshi woman who enters an arranged marriage with Chanu Ahmed in Tower Hamlets, East London?
questions.explanation: Shortlisted for the 2003 Booker Prize Monica Ali Brick Lane traces Nazneen quiet emancipation in the Bangladeshi community of East London.

questions.question: Which of the following statements concerning British literature from 1945 to the present is NOT correct?
options: Salman Rushdie's 'Midnight's Children' won the Booker Prize in 1981
Samuel Beckett was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1969
The Theatres Act of 1968 abolished stage censorship by the Lord Chamberlain
William Golding won the inaugural Booker Prize in 1969 for his 1954 novel 'Lord of the Flies'
questions.explanation: The Booker Prize was not established until 1969 when P H Newby won; William Golding won the Booker Prize in 1980 for his sea novel Rites of Passage.

questions.question: Which of the following character-and-work pairings from the Postmodern and Contemporary Period (1945–present) is NOT correctly matched?
options: Saleem Sinai — Vikram Seth's 'A Suitable Boy'
Jimmy Porter — John Osborne's 'Look Back in Anger'
Charles Smithson — John Fowles's 'The French Lieutenant's Woman'
questions.explanation: Saleem Sinai is the protagonist of Salman Rushdie 1981 novel Midnight Children whereas Lata Mehra is the central heroine of Vikram Seth A Suitable Boy.
